newsitem.title: USA: Albright's siblings seek family ties in Prague.
newsitem.headline: Albright's siblings seek family ties in Prague.

text.p: New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's siblings are in Prague pursuing recent surprise disclosures that their family was Jewish and their relatives died in the Holocaust, an aide said on Thursday.

John Korbel, Albright's brother, and Kathy Silva, her sister, left the United States on Wednesday for the capital of the Czech Republic aiming to examine documents and talk to relatives there, the aide told Reuters.

The Washington Post, working with documents and interviews of friends and relatives, reported last week that Albright, who was born in Prague as Maria Jana Korbelova and was raised a Roman Catholic, was actually of Jewish heritage. Three of her grandparents died in the Holocaust, the newspaper said.

The story about how one family coped with Nazism has spawned a flurry of follow-up media reports. It has stirred a debate over whether Albright's parents made the right choice in falsifying a new background for their children and whether Albright should have more vigorously pursued hints in recent years that her family's history may have been different from what she believed.
"This is a very personal issue and I am dealing with it in a personal way," Albright told Reuters in an interview.

"I think that what is most important here now is that I roll up my sleeves and be secretary of state, that is what I was hired to do," she said in her private office on the State Department's seventh-floor executive suite.

She said she had not tried to contact a cousin, Dagmar Simova, who spoke to the Post about Albright's past, since the story broke. But an aide said Albright's siblings would try to see the woman on their visit to the Czech Republic.

After the Post story first appeared, Albright called the revelations "fairly compelling." The State Department on Thursday accepted the findings as definitive, saying in recent days, "there's been a rush of information available to her ... so the weight of the evidence seems to be quite clear here."

Interviewed two days before she leaves on her first overseas trip as secretary of state -- a whirlwind 11-day tour of major European and Asian capitals -- Albright said the media frenzy over her heritage has not prevented her from doing her new job.
But she seemed eager to refocus the spotlight from this moving family saga to her new role as America's top diplomat.

"I truly do think what is important to think about here is this is an incredible country where people came and come in order to have the possibility of following one's personal life, where there is tolerance, optimism and generosity, and that I would hope that I would be given a chance to pursue my job in a way that i think is best," she said.
Albright, daughter of a Czech diplomat and academic, spent wartime with her family in London. She attended school in Switzerland at age 10 and acquired the name Madeleine.
Her father, Josef Korbel, left his homeland with his family after the communist takeover in 1948 and got a teaching job in Denver, Colorado.

Albright has said previously that the news about her Jewish background "was a major surprise to me," and that she was grateful to her parents, whom she revered but are not deceased, for making a difficult decision.
